questions.explanation: She first watches nervously for signs of boredom, then sees the audience go still and finds herself caught up with them.

questions.passage: Lake Mead, about 40 kilometers east of Las Vegas, was created in the 1930s when the Hoover Dam was built across the Colorado River. Today, the reservoir serves several purposes. Its dam produces hydroelectric power, its water irrigates farmland downstream, and its shores attract thousands of visitors each summer who come to swim, boat, and fish.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Lake Mead is the largest lake in the United States.
Building the Hoover Dam was difficult and expensive.
Lake Mead serves several purposes, from producing electricity to offering a place for recreation.
Summers in Las Vegas have become hotter in recent years.
questions.explanation: The text says the reservoir "serves several purposes" and then lists them: power, irrigation, and recreation.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a short story. Ben has just finished his first season as a goalkeeper on a youth soccer team.

Ben had let in eleven goals in his first five games, and after each one he had replayed the ball's path in his mind until he fell asleep. By the end of the season, he still let in goals, but fewer, and he had stopped replaying them. Instead, he found himself thinking about the shots he had stopped: the low one in the rain, the one that stung his palms, the one his teammates still talked about.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ben decides to stop playing goalkeeper.
Ben's teammates blame him for the team's losses.
Ben cannot remember the details of his games.
Over the season, Ben shifts from dwelling on his mistakes to remembering his successes.
questions.explanation: Early on he replays the goals he let in; by the end he thinks "instead" about the shots he stopped.

questions.passage: Many migratory songbirds fly at night and rest during the day. One long-standing explanation is that cooler night air helps them avoid overheating during long flights. Ornithologist Lucy Hartmann proposes an additional reason: by flying at night, birds keep the daylight hours free for feeding, so they can refuel at a stopover site each day without losing travel time. Her observations of warblers at stopover sites in southern Italy showed that the birds spent most of each day feeding before resuming their journey after dark.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: A researcher has shown that cooler night air is not the reason songbirds migrate at night.
A researcher suggests that flying at night may benefit songbirds not only by keeping them cool but also by leaving the day free for feeding.
Songbirds would rather migrate during the day but are forced to fly at night by high temperatures.
Warblers that stop in southern Italy migrate shorter distances than other songbirds.
questions.explanation: Hartmann offers an **additional** reason, so she adds to the cooling explanation rather than rejecting it, as the first choice claims.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a short story. Antonio is a retired stage actor.

Antonio had played the old king in *The Winter Orchard* more than two hundred times, and in his youth he had thought it a dull role: the king spends most of the play seated on his throne, listening while others argue. Now, watching a young actor rehearse the part, Antonio noticed how much the young man was trying to do: frowning, pacing, waving his hands. "Let them come to you," Antonio said at last. "The king's power is that he doesn't need to move."
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Experience has led Antonio to value a quality of the role that he once considered a weakness.
Antonio is jealous of the young actor who now plays the old king.
Antonio believes that *The Winter Orchard* is a poorly written play.
Antonio regrets that he never had the chance to play the old king.
questions.explanation: As a young man he found the king's stillness dull; now he sees that stillness as the source of the king's power.

questions.passage: Along the Rio Grande in New Mexico, narrow strips of forest called bosque grow on land that floods each spring. The cottonwoods and willows of these forests depend on the floods to soak their roots and to carry their seeds to fresh ground. Where dams and canals have stopped the yearly floods, bosque forests have thinned and, in some places, disappeared.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Bosque forests contain more tree species than any other forest in North America.
Dams on the Rio Grande were built mainly to protect bosque forests.
Cottonwoods grow faster than willows along the Rio Grande.
Bosque forests along the Rio Grande depend on yearly floods and decline when those floods stop.
questions.explanation: The text explains that bosque trees need the spring floods and then shows what happens to the forests when the floods are stopped.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a short story. Years after leaving her village, Maeve hears a bodhrán, a frame drum, at a wedding in the city.

Maeve had not thought of her grandmother's drum in years. But as the bodhrán player struck the first sharp beats, she felt her hands lift slightly from her lap, as though they still remembered the rhythms her grandmother had tapped out on winter evenings. Around her, the guests clapped along, unaware that for Maeve the bright hall had briefly become a small kitchen two hundred kilometers away.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Maeve regrets that she never learned to play the bodhrán well.
The sound of the drum brings back vivid memories of Maeve's childhood with her grandmother.
Maeve feels uncomfortable among the wedding guests in the city.
Maeve is surprised that the guests know the rhythms her grandmother played.
questions.explanation: The drumbeats make her hands "remember" her grandmother's rhythms and carry her back to the kitchen of her childhood.

questions.passage: Papermaking reached Fabriano, Italy, by the thirteenth century, and the town soon became famous for its paper. Workers there made paper from linen rags, producing sheets that were smooth and strong. Merchants carried Fabriano paper to cities across Europe, where it gradually replaced more expensive writing materials such as parchment.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Paper was invented in Fabriano in the thirteenth century.
Fabriano became an important center of papermaking, and its paper spread widely.
Parchment lasted longer than the paper made in Fabriano.
Merchants in Fabriano preferred parchment to paper.
questions.explanation: The text explains how Fabriano became known for paper and how that paper spread to other cities. Papermaking "reached" the town; it was not invented there.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a short story. Felix is spending the day helping his aunt in her bookbinding shop.

Felix had expected the work to be dull. Instead, he found himself watching his aunt's hands: the quick fold of each sheet, the needle pulled through in a single smooth motion, the tap of the bone folder that pressed every crease flat. By evening he had stitched his first small notebook, crooked but whole, and he held it the way he might have held a prize.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Felix's aunt is disappointed by the notebook he makes.
Felix decides that bookbinding is too difficult for him to learn.
Felix finds the bookbinding work more absorbing than he expected and takes pride in what he makes.
Felix would rather read books than make them.
questions.explanation: He expected dull work but was fascinated, and he holds his notebook "the way he might have held a prize."

questions.passage: When people recall an event, they do not simply replay a stored record. Instead, each act of remembering partly rebuilds the memory, and details supplied by later experiences can be woven into it. Psychologist Alex Romero argues that this helps explain a puzzle about eyewitnesses: their accounts often become more detailed and more confident over repeated interviews, even as the event itself recedes further into the past.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Eyewitnesses become less confident in their memories the more often they are interviewed.
Memories of events are stored as exact records that can be replayed later.
A psychologist argues that the way memories are rebuilt each time they are recalled can explain why eyewitness accounts grow more detailed over time.
Repeated interviews help eyewitnesses recover details of an event that they had at first forgotten.
questions.explanation: The text explains that remembering rebuilds memories and uses this to explain growing detail in eyewitness accounts. The last choice is tempting, but the text says new details come from later experiences, not that forgotten details are recovered.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker describes a river in late summer.

The river has forgotten its spring voice,
the roar that tore the willows from the bank;
now it moves like an old man counting coins,
slow, careful, sure of every one it keeps.
Yet underneath the stillness, in the reeds,
a hundred lives are feeding on its patience.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Though the river has lost the force it had in spring, its slow summer flow quietly supports abundant life.
The speaker regrets the damage that the river caused to the willows in spring.
The speaker compares the river to an old man in order to suggest that it will soon dry up.
The river is more dangerous in late summer than it appears to be.
questions.explanation: The poem contrasts the roaring spring river with its calm summer flow and ends with the "hundred lives" it feeds. The old man is careful and "sure," not dying, so nothing suggests the river will dry up.

questions.passage: Manatees are large, slow-moving mammals that graze on sea grasses and other plants in warm coastal waters. Despite their size, they have little body fat for insulation and a slow metabolism, so they cannot tolerate cold water for long. When winter temperatures fall, many manatees in Florida swim to natural springs or to the warm water released by power plants, where they gather in large groups until the weather warms.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Manatees eat more plants in winter than in summer.
Power plants have caused manatee populations to decline.
Manatees prefer to live alone except during the breeding season.
Because manatees are sensitive to cold, many of them seek out warm water when temperatures drop.
questions.explanation: The text explains why manatees can't handle cold and then describes how they move to warm water in winter.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a short story. Isabel has returned to her grandmother's village in Tuscany for the first time in ten years.

The road was paved now, and a shop with a bright plastic sign stood where the old bakery had been. Isabel walked past houses she did not recognize, feeling like a visitor in someone else's memory. Then she reached the end of the lane and saw it: the mulberry tree in her grandmother's courtyard, its branches still bent low over the wall, exactly as tall as she remembered.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Isabel is disappointed to learn that her grandmother has cut down the mulberry tree.
Isabel regrets returning to the village after so many years away.
Although much of the village feels unfamiliar to Isabel, she finds something that has stayed the same.
Isabel is pleased that the village has become more modern.
questions.explanation: Most details show change (paved road, new shop, unknown houses), but the mulberry tree is "exactly as" she remembered.

questions.passage: Jerboas are small rodents that live in the deserts of North Africa and Arabia. Their long back legs let them hop quickly across loose sand, and their long tails help them keep their balance as they leap. Many jerboas also have large ears that help release body heat. These features help jerboas survive in hot, open desert environments.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Jerboas have several physical features that help them live in the desert.
Jerboas are the fastest animals in the Sahara.
Jerboas live only in North Africa.
Jerboas use their tails mainly to dig burrows.
questions.explanation: The text lists the jerboa's legs, tail, and ears and says these features help it survive in the desert.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a short story. Lucía is learning a traditional dance from her aunt.

Aunt Carmen stopped the music in the middle of the song. "Your feet are perfect," she said, "but your hands are asleep." She lifted Lucía's wrist and turned it slowly, so that the fingers opened like petals. "In this dance, the hands tell the story. The feet only carry it."
questions.prompt: According to the text, why does Aunt Carmen stop the music?
choices: She thinks Lucía's footwork needs more practice.
She has decided that the song is too difficult for Lucía.
She wants Lucía to make her hand movements more expressive.
She wants to show Lucía a new set of steps.
questions.explanation: She praises Lucía's feet but says her "hands are asleep," then shows her how to move them. The problem is the hands, not the feet.

questions.passage: In the coastal waters of the northeastern Pacific, two kinds of orcas often swim within sight of each other yet rarely interact. So-called resident orcas eat mainly fish, especially salmon, and travel in large, noisy groups. Bigg's orcas hunt seals and other marine mammals, travel in small groups, and stay largely silent while hunting, perhaps because their prey can hear them. Genetic studies show that the two groups have not interbred for many thousands of years, suggesting that differences in diet and behavior, rather than physical barriers, have kept them apart.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Two groups of orcas that share the same waters have remained separate, apparently because of differences in what they eat and how they behave.
Resident orcas and Bigg's orcas differ in diet, but genetic studies show that they often interbreed.
Bigg's orcas are kept apart from resident orcas mainly by physical barriers in the northeastern Pacific.
Bigg's orcas hunt more successfully than resident orcas because they stay silent while hunting.
questions.explanation: The text describes differences in diet and behavior and ends with genetic evidence that these differences, not barriers, keep the groups apart. The silence detail supports that point, and the text never compares hunting success.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker is addressing a dancer.

You say the dance is over when the drum goes still,
but I have watched you walk home afterward:
the way you lift your wrist to wave goodbye,
the way you turn at the gate, half a beat behind
some music only you can hear.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker regrets that the dancer no longer performs in public.
The speaker criticizes the dancer for leaving before the music has finished.
The speaker suggests that the dancer has trouble keeping time with the drum during performances.
The speaker suggests that the dancer's everyday movements are still shaped by dance after the performance has ended.
questions.explanation: The dancer says the dance ends with the drum, but the speaker sees dance-like gestures and an inner rhythm on the walk home. "Half a beat behind" describes that walk, not a problem during a performance.

questions.passage: In Siena, Italy, daily life is shaped by the contrada, a neighborhood community whose members tend to know one another well. Neighbors in a contrada often help one another prepare for weddings, work together to get ready for the Palio, the city's twice-yearly horse race, and gather at the contrada's social club to discuss neighborhood matters. In this way, the contrada gives city dwellers the kind of close ties often associated with village life.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The contrada gives city residents close community ties through shared activities and mutual help.
Contrade are found only in the oldest parts of Italian cities.
Social clubs are the most important buildings in Siena's neighborhoods.
Most residents of Siena would prefer to live in villages.
questions.explanation: The text lists ways neighbors in a contrada help and meet one another, then concludes that the contrada gives city dwellers village-like close ties.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a short story. Ingrid is restoring a damaged painting in a museum workshop.

For three weeks Ingrid had worked on a single patch of sky no larger than her palm, lifting away a century of grime with cotton swabs she rolled herself. Visitors who passed the workshop window sometimes stopped, waiting for something to happen, and then wandered on. She did not mind. Each evening, when she switched off her lamp, the blue was a little truer than it had been that morning, and that was enough.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ingrid is frustrated that visitors do not appreciate her work.
Ingrid worries that she will not finish restoring the painting on time.
Ingrid has decided to stop working on the painting's sky.
Ingrid is content with her slow, gradual progress, even though others see little happening.
questions.explanation: Visitors see nothing happening, but "She did not mind": the small daily improvement in the blue "was enough" for her.

questions.passage: In a tropical rainforest, the canopy, the layer formed by the crowns of the tallest trees, blocks most sunlight from reaching the forest floor. As a result, many plants on the forest floor have broad, thin leaves that capture as much of the dim light as possible, and some young trees grow very slowly for years, waiting until a fallen tree opens a gap in the canopy above them.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The tallest trees in a rainforest grow faster than any other plants.
Plants on the rainforest floor have ways of coping with the low light caused by the canopy.
Fallen trees are the main cause of damage to rainforest plants.
Rainforest plants with broad leaves need less water than other plants.
questions.explanation: The canopy causes low light, and both examples (broad leaves and slow-growing young trees) show how plants below cope with it.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker describes a canal in a village.

The canal is older than the village road,
older than the mosque's blue door, older
than anyone who drinks from it. Each spring
it remembers the mountains and comes running,
carrying snow that fell before I was born
to the roots of my grandmother's apricot trees.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker worries that the canal will soon run dry.
The speaker explains how the villagers built the canal.
The speaker presents the canal as an ancient presence that still links the distant mountains to life in the village.
The speaker prefers the village road to the canal.
questions.explanation: The canal is "older" than everything in the village, and each spring it still carries mountain snow to the village's trees, linking the two.

questions.passage: Forest managers once treated dead and dying trees as a sign of an unhealthy forest and often cut them down to slow the spread of insects and disease. Many ecologists now see these standing dead trees, called snags, differently. Woodpeckers carve nest holes in their soft wood, and the same holes are later used by owls, bats, and squirrels that cannot dig their own. Meanwhile, fungi and beetles that break down the wood return nutrients to the soil. Removing snags, in this view, may protect some living trees while weakening the forest as a whole.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Dead trees, once seen mainly as a threat to forest health, are increasingly recognized as valuable to the wider forest ecosystem.
Forest managers should never remove dead trees, even when insects threaten nearby living trees.
Snags are valuable mainly because woodpeckers use them for nesting.
Insects and disease spread more quickly in forests that contain many dead trees.
questions.explanation: The text contrasts the old view of snags as a threat with the newer view that they support many species and the soil. *Never remove* goes further than the text, and the woodpecker choice is only one detail.

questions.passage:
The following text is from a short story. Paolo has returned to his family's orchard after several years of working in the city.

His father walked him down the rows without speaking, stopping now and then to lay a hand on a trunk the way another man might greet a neighbor. On the train, Paolo had rehearsed a speech about drip lines and new varieties that could double the harvest. Watching his father's hand move over the rough bark, he found that he could no longer remember how it began.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Paolo realizes that the orchard is failing and must be modernized quickly.
Paolo's father is angry that Paolo left the orchard to work in the city.
Paolo forgets his speech because he is exhausted from the long train journey.
Seeing how deeply his father is attached to the trees makes Paolo unsure about proposing the changes he had planned.
questions.explanation: The father greets the trees like neighbors, and watching this, Paolo loses hold of his speech about changing the orchard. The text gives no sign of tiredness, so forgetting reflects his doubt, not exhaustion.

questions.passage: In the 1950s, chemist Rosalind Park began collecting samples of rainwater from the roof of her laboratory every week. She was not testing any particular idea; she simply wanted a record. Decades later, other scientists used her samples to show how air pollution in the region had changed over time, a question Park herself had never set out to answer.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Park's habit of collecting rainwater produced a record that later proved valuable for research she had not planned.
Park designed an experiment to measure changes in air pollution.
Rainwater samples are the most reliable way to study air pollution.
Park's colleagues disagreed about how to store her rainwater samples.
questions.explanation: The text stresses that Park collected samples without a specific goal, yet the record later answered a question about pollution. She did not design a pollution experiment, and the text makes no claim that rainwater is the most reliable method.

questions.passage: Honeybees perform a "waggle dance" to tell their hivemates where flowers are. The angle of the dance shows the direction of the food relative to the Sun, and the length of the waggle shows the distance. Researchers in Germany recently found that young bees' dances are often imprecise, with noticeable errors in angle. The errors shrank as the bees gained experience, suggesting that the dance is partly learned by watching older bees, not entirely inborn.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Honeybees can communicate only the direction of food, not its distance.
Young honeybees find food more quickly than older bees do.
Research suggests that honeybees' ability to perform the waggle dance accurately improves with experience and learning.
Honeybees perform the waggle dance only in Germany.
questions.explanation: The key finding is that young bees' dances start imprecise and improve, which points to learning. The text says the dance shows both direction and distance, and it says nothing about how fast bees find food.

questions.passage: The Atacama Desert in Chile is one of the driest places on Earth. Some weather stations there have never recorded rain. Because the air is so dry and clear, and because the land is high and far from city lights, astronomers have built several major telescopes in the desert to observe the night sky.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The Atacama Desert receives more rain than most deserts.
The Atacama Desert's dry, clear conditions make it a good place for telescopes.
Astronomers prefer working in cities to working in deserts.
Weather stations in Chile are often broken.
questions.explanation: The text explains that dry, clear air and distance from city lights led astronomers to build telescopes in the Atacama. It states the opposite of the first choice and says nothing about broken stations.

questions.passage: In the 1800s, many cities in Europe and North America covered small rivers with streets and buildings, turning them into underground drains. In recent decades, some cities have reversed this process, a practice called "daylighting." Seoul, South Korea, for example, removed an elevated highway and uncovered the Cheonggyecheon stream in 2005. The restored stream now draws visitors, provides habitat for fish and birds, and helps cool the surrounding neighborhood.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Seoul was the first city to build streets over small rivers.
Most cities have already uncovered all of their buried rivers.
Underground drains are cheaper to maintain than open streams.
Some cities are uncovering buried streams, which can bring several benefits.
questions.explanation: The text describes "daylighting," gives Seoul as an example, and lists benefits of the restored stream. It does not say Seoul was first to bury rivers, that most cities have finished, or compare costs.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from a 1921 novel. Theo has returned to his hometown after many years.
The main street was wider than he remembered and lined with shops whose names he did not know. Yet when he turned the corner by the church, the old elm still stood at the bend of the road, its trunk scarred where he and his brother had carved their initials, and for a moment he felt that he had never gone away at all.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Theo regrets having carved his initials into the elm tree.
Theo is pleased that the town has grown larger and more modern.
Although much of the town has changed, a familiar landmark makes Theo feel briefly connected to his past.
Theo cannot find the church he attended as a child.
questions.explanation: The street and shops are unfamiliar, but seeing the old elm makes him feel "he had never gone away at all." The text expresses no regret or pleasure about the changes, and he finds the church easily.

questions.passage: Many people assume that octopuses, being solitary animals, have little use for social skills. But a study in a bay off the coast of Australia found a site where dozens of gloomy octopuses lived close together, sharing dens and frequently interacting. The researchers observed octopuses signaling to one another by changing their color and posture, and even evicting one another from dens. They suggest that octopuses may be more socially flexible than previously thought, capable of living in groups when conditions such as abundant food and limited shelter bring them together.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Research at one site suggests that octopuses can adapt to living in groups under certain conditions.
Gloomy octopuses are the only octopuses that change color.
Octopuses in Australia are more intelligent than octopuses elsewhere.
Most octopuses prefer to share dens with other octopuses.
questions.explanation: The study at one site found octopuses living and interacting in groups, leading researchers to suggest that octopuses are socially flexible when conditions allow. The text does not claim most octopuses prefer sharing or compare intelligence.

questions.passage: In 1928, Alexander Fleming returned from a vacation to find that mold had grown in one of his dishes of bacteria. Around the mold, the bacteria had died. Rather than throwing the dish away, Fleming studied the mold and found that it produced a substance that killed many kinds of bacteria. That substance, penicillin, later became one of the most important medicines in history.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Fleming went on vacation to study mold in a different country.
Molds are more dangerous than bacteria.
Penicillin was difficult to produce in large amounts.
Fleming's careful attention to an accident led to the discovery of an important medicine.
questions.explanation: The text describes how an unexpected mold growth, which Fleming chose to study, led to penicillin. It says nothing about production difficulties, and Fleming studied the mold after returning, not on vacation.

questions.passage: Some animals that live in caves, such as certain fish and salamanders, have lost the ability to see. For a long time, biologists thought this happened simply because unused eyes slowly wasted away over generations. More recent research suggests another reason: building and running eyes requires a great deal of energy. In the darkness of a cave, where food is scarce, animals that do not spend energy on eyes may survive better than those that do.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Cave animals can see better in darkness than animals that live above ground.
Recent research suggests that cave animals may have lost their sight partly because eyes cost energy that is valuable when food is scarce.
Most cave animals are fish or salamanders.
Biologists now agree that eyes are not important to any animals.
questions.explanation: The text contrasts an older explanation with a newer one: eyes use energy, and saving that energy helps where food is scarce. It does not claim cave animals see well, and it says nothing to suggest eyes are unimportant to all animals.

questions.passage: Mount Everest grows a few millimeters taller every year. This happens because the Indian tectonic plate, a huge slab of Earth's crust, keeps pushing slowly into the Eurasian plate. The pressure where the two plates meet forces the land upward, raising the Himalaya mountains, including Everest.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Mount Everest is the most difficult mountain to climb.
The Himalaya mountains are shrinking because of erosion.
Mount Everest keeps growing because two tectonic plates are pushing against each other.
The Indian plate is moving away from the Eurasian plate.
questions.explanation: The text explains that Everest grows because the Indian plate pushes into the Eurasian plate. It says the plates are pushing together, not moving apart, and says nothing about climbing difficulty.

questions.passage: In the 1800s, many people believed that the stripes of a zebra helped it hide in tall grass. Recent studies point to another purpose. When researchers dressed horses in striped coats, biting flies landed on them far less often than on horses in plain coats. The flies seemed to have trouble landing on striped surfaces, which suggests that stripes may protect zebras from insect bites, and from the diseases those insects carry.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Recent research suggests that zebra stripes may help protect zebras from biting flies.
Horses and zebras are closely related animals.
Zebra stripes help zebras hide from lions in tall grass.
Biting flies prefer horses to zebras.
questions.explanation: The text presents an experiment suggesting stripes keep biting flies away. Choice C is the older belief that the text moves away from, and the text does not compare flies' preferences between species.

questions.passage:
The following text is adapted from a 1913 novel. Eleanor, a young teacher, has arrived in a small mountain village.
The children stared at her from the doorway as if she were some strange bird blown in by the storm. Eleanor smiled at them, though her heart beat fast, and said she had brought a book of stories with pictures in it. One small boy edged forward, then another, and before the kettle had boiled, three of them were crowded around her chair, their wariness forgotten in their eagerness to see what came next.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Eleanor is unhappy about being sent to a village so far from home.
Eleanor wins over the curious but cautious children by sharing a picture book.
The children are frightened by the storm and seek shelter in Eleanor's house.
Eleanor believes the children have never seen a book before.
questions.explanation: The children are wary at first but crowd around Eleanor once she offers stories with pictures. The text does not say she is unhappy, that the children fear the storm, or what she believes about their experience with books.

questions.passage: Bird migration has long puzzled scientists, partly because birds often fly at night and over oceans, where they are hard to observe. Over the last decade, researchers have attached tiny tracking devices, some weighing less than a gram, to birds as small as warblers. The data have revealed that many small birds fly far longer distances without stopping than anyone had expected, sometimes crossing an ocean in a single flight of more than two days.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Scientists still have no way to track small birds during migration.
Most migrating birds fly only during the day.
Tiny tracking devices have shown that small migrating birds can make much longer nonstop flights than researchers expected.
Warblers are the smallest birds that migrate over oceans.
questions.explanation: The text describes how tiny trackers revealed unexpectedly long nonstop flights by small birds. Choice A contradicts the text, and the text says birds often fly at night.

questions.passage: In 1953, Edmund Hillary of New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay of Nepal became the first people known to reach the summit of Mount Everest. Their success depended on the work of a large team. Hundreds of porters carried supplies up the mountain, and other climbers set up a series of camps so that the two men could make the final climb.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The first known climb to the top of Everest relied on the efforts of many people, not just the two who reached the summit.
Hillary and Norgay climbed Everest alone and without supplies.
Mount Everest is the tallest mountain in New Zealand.
Most people who climb Everest today do not use porters.

I had desired it with an ardour that far exceeded moderation; but now that I had finished, the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

Victor plans to begin a new project to restore his health.
Victor is proud that he sacrificed his health for science.
Victor's long-awaited success brings him horror instead of satisfaction.
questions.explanation: After two years of obsessive work, "the beauty of the dream vanished" and "horror and disgust" filled him. His success brings horror, not satisfaction.

questions.passage: Economists use the term "Dutch disease" for a pattern in which a boom in one export, such as natural gas, raises the value of a country's currency, making its other exports more expensive abroad and therefore less competitive. The name refers to the Netherlands' experience after the discovery of a vast gas field there in 1959. Some economists argue, however, that the pattern is not inevitable: a country that saves much of its resource income in foreign investments, rather than spending it at home, can limit the rise in its currency.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the main topic of the text?
choices: The history of natural gas production in the Netherlands since 1959
A way that success in one industry can harm others, and how that harm might be limited
Reasons that a country's currency can lose value after a resource boom
Why economists disagree about whether natural gas exports are profitable
questions.explanation: The text defines a pattern in which one booming export hurts other exports, then describes a way to limit it. A is just the example; C reverses the effect (the currency gains value).

questions.passage: Within higher education, studying philosophy requires that students be conversant with the field's foundational texts and historical figures. By contrast, doing philosophy within or beyond the academy demands the creative, self-directed application of acquired expertise to enduring questions about the nature of existence and knowledge. While both approaches engage with influential figures, those who do philosophy treat such figures as vital interlocutors who facilitate new insights rather than as ossified authorities who, though relevant to the present, primarily represent the discipline's past.
questions.prompt: Based on the text, which choice best describes the relationship between doing philosophy and studying philosophy?
choices: Doing philosophy represents a departure from the norms that govern scholarly inquiry, whereas studying philosophy requires conformation to these norms.
Doing philosophy involves developing novel ideas through imagined dialogue with past philosophers based on knowledge of those philosophers' views acquired by studying philosophy.
Doing philosophy helps students formulate concrete solutions to practical issues, whereas studying philosophy prioritizes engagement with historical arguments in the field.
Doing philosophy requires students to challenge the ideas articulated by past philosophers, especially when these ideas are broadly accepted by other people studying philosophy.
questions.explanation: Doing philosophy applies "acquired expertise" (from studying) and treats past figures as "interlocutors who facilitate new insights." That is developing new ideas through a kind of dialogue with past thinkers, built on what studying provides.
